description: Team Mysterio is six problem-solvers who believe space education shouldn't feel like a textbook. Some kids learn by playing, some by reading, some by listening. So we built Jr_AstroCamp, an edtech platform.
summary:
Jr_AstroCamp is a browser-based space-science learning platform for young students, built by Team Mysterio from Bangladesh. Students play a game built on 76 historical NASA missions, then take on four survival missions, two on the Moon and two on Mars, where they manage oxygen, water, food and power and see how each decision affects the crew. After each attempt they can review the outcome and try again. From Start Learning, they choose a short video, audio lesson, comic, handwritten-style notes, or gameplay, so every learner has a way in. NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day, near-Earth asteroid feed, Image and Video Library, and a Moonquake Map add live and archival context, while cited NASA sources inform simplified, not operational, simulations.

It answers the challenge to build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer by making the mission itself the classroom. Space content is often too simple or too technical and students rarely get to fail safely and learn from it. Jr_AstroCamp gives them that chance.
details:
Jr_AstroCamp is a browser-based space STEM learning experience created for NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. It puts students in the role of a mission crew member: they explore a mission, make decisions, see what happens, and then learn more in a format that works for them.

Space science can feel distant to beginners and learning only through reading or quizzes may not work for everyone. Jr_AstroCamp aims to make mission concepts more approachable without removing the problem-solving and tradeoffs that make space exploration challenging. Students can experiment, make mistakes safely, and try again.

The browser app includes a campaign of 76 curated historical NASA mission profiles, covering topics such as launch, docking, landing, rover operations, telescopes, and deep-space exploration. A student can review a mission briefing, make a decision during an interactive experience, and consider the result afterward. The app also includes four survival scenarios, two on the Moon and two on Mars, in which students manage oxygen, water, food and power. These choices introduce systems thinking: changing one resource or priority can affect the rest of the mission.

Start Learning gives students five ways to explore a topic: gameplay, video lessons, audio lessons, comics, and handwritten-style notes. Students can choose how they want to engage rather than being limited to one format. The app also includes a NASA Live Observatory with NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day and Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs) information, the ISS’s current position from the third-party Where the ISS at API, and search through the NASA Image and Video Library.

A 3D Moonquake Map plots bundled Apollo seismic-event references based on the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment archive. Its animated waveform is illustrative, not a recorded seismic trace. NASA references also inform selected educational scenarios, including the BVAD report for simplified life-support decisions; LOLA and LCROSS references for lunar terrain and ice concepts; DONKI and CRaTER for solar-weather and radiation scenarios; and REMS, MEDA, MOLA, and KRUSTY for Mars and power context. These references help ground the learning experience, but the scenarios are simplified: they are not operational training, raw telemetry, or live environmental simulations. When an API request is unavailable, some views can use bundled sample content.

The project’s intended benefits are to encourage curiosity about space, give students practice making decisions, and help them understand how mission systems interact. Our intended impact is to make space learning more active and approachable for young learners. We have not yet measured classroom learning outcomes; the next step is to invite teachers and students to try the experience, gather feedback, and improve the missions and debriefs based on what they need.

We built the browser app with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js. Mission and scenario content is curated in the project, while selected NASA APIs provide separate live context when available. No specialized hardware is required. The local CapCom helper uses authored science notes and response rules; student questions are not sent to an external AI service.

Creativity in Jr_AstroCamp comes from combining mission-style decision-making with several learning formats in one browser experience. Students can move from a mission challenge to a video, comic, audio lesson, notes, or gameplay, then explore NASA imagery and selected space data. In designing the project, we considered beginner-friendly navigation, different ways of learning, the value of safe failure and retries, browser access, and scientific transparency. We distinguish live API content from bundled references and simplified game values so students can explore confidently without mistaking an educational simulation for real mission telemetry.
